column1: Why value closing stock at lower of cost or NRV (AS 2)?
column2: Prudence — never carry an asset above realisable cash; recognise a probable loss now but never an unrealised gain.

column1: Which AS governs Valuation of Inventories?
column2: AS 2 — inventories measured at lower of cost and net realisable value.

column1: What is Net Realisable Value under AS 2?
column2: Estimated selling price in ordinary course LESS estimated costs of completion and costs to make the sale.

column1: Which cost formulas does AS 2 permit?
column2: FIFO or Weighted Average; LIFO is prohibited because it distorts the balance sheet with outdated costs.

column1: What costs are excluded from inventory cost (AS 2)?
column2: Abnormal waste, storage (unless needed for production), admin overheads, and selling costs — they don't bring stock to present location/condition.

column1: Why are borrowing costs on a qualifying asset capitalised (AS 16)?
column2: They are directly attributable to acquiring an asset that takes substantial time to be ready; matching cost to future benefit.

column1: What is a qualifying asset under AS 16?
column2: An asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale.

column1: When must capitalisation of borrowing costs cease (AS 16)?
column2: When substantially all activities to prepare the asset for its intended use/sale are complete.

column1: Why suspend capitalisation of borrowing costs during extended interruption (AS 16)?
column2: No asset is being readied during idle periods, so continuing to capitalise would overstate the asset.

column1: Which AS deals with Depreciation Accounting principles now?
column2: AS 10 (Property, Plant & Equipment) — the old AS 6 was withdrawn and merged into AS 10.

column1: Why depreciate an asset (AS 10)?
column2: To allocate the depreciable amount systematically over useful life — matching the asset's consumption to revenue it helps earn.

column1: What is depreciable amount (AS 10)?
column2: Cost (or revalued amount) of the asset LESS its residual value.

column1: How is a change in depreciation method treated (AS 10)?
column2: As a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively — not retrospectively.

column1: Why can't routine repairs be capitalised (AS 10)?
column2: They only maintain the originally assessed standard of performance; they don't add future economic benefits.

column1: Which AS covers Revenue Recognition?
column2: AS 9 — revenue from sale of goods, rendering of services, and interest/royalties/dividends.

column1: When is revenue from sale of goods recognised (AS 9)?
column2: When significant risks and rewards of ownership pass to the buyer and no significant uncertainty exists on collectability.

column1: Why recognise dividend income only when the right to receive is established (AS 9)?
column2: Until declared, there is no certainty of inflow; recognising earlier would breach prudence and the realisation principle.

column1: How is interest revenue recognised under AS 9?
column2: On a time proportion basis considering the amount outstanding and the applicable rate.

column1: Which AS governs Contingencies and Events after the Balance Sheet Date?
column2: AS 4.

column1: What is an adjusting event under AS 4?
column2: An event after the balance sheet date giving evidence of conditions existing AT the balance sheet date — adjust the financials.

column1: Why are proposed dividends no longer a provision (AS 4 revised)?
column2: They are declared after the balance sheet date and aren't an obligation at year-end; disclose in notes only.

column1: Which AS covers Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies?
column2: AS 5.

column1: What is a prior period item (AS 5)?
column2: Income or expense arising from errors or omissions in prior periods' statements, disclosed separately so current profit isn't distorted.

column1: Why apply a change in accounting policy retrospectively/with disclosure (AS 5)?
column2: To keep comparability and reveal the impact so users aren't misled by a break in consistency.

column1: Which AS deals with The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates?
column2: AS 11.

column1: How is a foreign currency monetary item reported at year-end (AS 11)?
column2: At the closing rate; exchange differences go to the profit and loss statement.

column1: Why translate non-monetary items at historical rate (AS 11)?
column2: They are carried at past transaction values, so the rate at the transaction date preserves that historical measurement.

column1: Which AS covers Accounting for Government Grants?
column2: AS 12.

column1: Why not recognise a government grant until reasonable assurance exists (AS 12)?
column2: Prudence — the enterprise must be reasonably certain it will comply with conditions and actually receive the grant.

column1: How is a grant related to a depreciable asset treated (AS 12)?
column2: Either deducted from asset cost or as deferred income released to P&L over the asset's useful life, matching the depreciation.

column1: How is a grant in the nature of promoters' contribution treated (AS 12)?
column2: Credited to capital reserve — it is not earned income and shouldn't inflate profit.

column1: Which AS covers Accounting for Investments?
column2: AS 13.

column1: How are current investments valued (AS 13)?
column2: Lower of cost and fair value — prudence, since they are held for short-term realisation.

column1: How are long-term investments valued (AS 13)?
column2: At cost, less any provision for a decline that is other than temporary.

column1: Why not write down a temporary fall in a long-term investment (AS 13)?
column2: The intent is long-term holding; short-term market swings don't reflect a permanent loss of value.

column1: Which AS governs Amalgamations?
column2: AS 14.

column1: Difference between amalgamation in nature of merger vs purchase (AS 14)?
column2: Merger: all five conditions met, pooling of interests; Purchase: any condition fails, use the purchase method.

column1: Under pooling of interests method, how are assets recorded (AS 14)?
column2: At existing book values; the difference on adjusting reserves goes to reserves, not goodwill.

column1: Under purchase method, how is the excess of consideration over net assets treated (AS 14)?
column2: As goodwill, amortised generally over a period not exceeding 5 years.

column1: What is purchase consideration under AS 14?
column2: The aggregate of shares and other securities issued plus payment made to shareholders of the transferor company (not to creditors).

column1: Which AS covers Employee Benefits?
column2: AS 15.

column1: Difference between defined contribution and defined benefit plan (AS 15)?
column2: Contribution: employer's obligation is the fixed contribution; Benefit: employer bears actuarial and investment risk of the promised benefit.

column1: Which AS covers Segment Reporting?
column2: AS 17.

column1: Which AS covers Related Party Disclosures?
column2: AS 18.

column1: Which AS covers Leases?
column2: AS 19.

column1: Finance vs operating lease — the deciding test (AS 19)?
column2: Finance lease transfers substantially all risks and rewards of ownership; otherwise it is an operating lease — substance over form.

column1: How does a lessee record a finance lease (AS 19)?
column2: As an asset and a liability at the lower of fair value and present value of minimum lease payments.

column1: Which AS covers Earnings Per Share?
column2: AS 20.

column1: Why compute diluted EPS (AS 20)?
column2: To show the worst-case earnings dilution if all potential equity shares (options, convertibles) were exercised.

column1: Basic EPS formula (AS 20)?
column2: Net profit attributable to equity shareholders divided by weighted average number of equity shares outstanding.

column1: Which AS covers Consolidated Financial Statements?
column2: AS 21.

column1: When does control exist for consolidation (AS 21)?
column2: More than half the voting power, or control of the composition of the board of directors.

column1: Why eliminate intra-group transactions on consolidation (AS 21)?
column2: The group is a single economic entity; unrealised internal profits and mutual balances would overstate group results.

column1: How is minority interest shown in consolidated balance sheet (AS 21)?
column2: Separately from the parent's equity and liabilities — it belongs to outside shareholders of the subsidiary.

column1: Which AS covers Accounting for Taxes on Income?
column2: AS 22.

column1: Why create deferred tax (AS 22)?
column2: To match tax expense with accounting profit despite timing differences between book and taxable income.

column1: When is a deferred tax asset recognised (AS 22)?
column2: Only when there is reasonable (or virtual, for unabsorbed losses) certainty of future taxable income to realise it — prudence.

column1: Difference: timing vs permanent differences (AS 22)?
column2: Timing differences reverse in future periods (create deferred tax); permanent differences never reverse (no deferred tax).

column1: Which AS covers Investments in Associates in Consolidated Statements?
column2: AS 23 — uses the equity method.

column1: What is an associate (AS 23)?
column2: An enterprise in which the investor has significant influence (usually 20% or more voting power) but not control.

column1: How does the equity method work (AS 23)?
column2: Investment recorded at cost, then adjusted for the investor's share of post-acquisition profits or losses.

column1: Which AS covers Discontinuing Operations?
column2: AS 24.

column1: Which AS covers Interim Financial Reporting?
column2: AS 25.

column1: Which AS covers Intangible Assets?
column2: AS 26.

column1: Why is internally generated goodwill not recognised (AS 26)?
column2: It isn't identifiable or reliably measurable and isn't a resource controlled from a past transaction.

column1: Research vs development expenditure treatment (AS 26)?
column2: Research is always expensed; development is capitalised only if strict feasibility and future-benefit criteria are met.

column1: Which AS covers Financial Reporting of Interests in Joint Ventures?
column2: AS 27 — uses proportionate consolidation for jointly controlled entities.

column1: Which AS covers Impairment of Assets?
column2: AS 28.

column1: What is an impairment loss (AS 28)?
column2: The excess of an asset's carrying amount over its recoverable amount.

column1: Which AS covers Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets?
column2: AS 29.

column1: When is a provision recognised (AS 29)?
column2: A present obligation from a past event, probable outflow of resources, and a reliable estimate can be made.

column1: Why are contingent assets not recognised (AS 29)?
column2: Prudence — recognising a possible gain not yet realised would overstate income; disclose only if inflow is probable.

column1: Why is a buy-back of shares done, and where does the premium go?
column2: To return surplus cash / improve EPS; premium on buy-back is charged to free reserves or securities premium.

column1: What does the Capital Redemption Reserve protect on buy-back/redemption?
column2: Creditors' cushion — capital reduced by buy-back is replaced by transferring an equal amount from free reserves to CRR.

column1: Buy-back limit under the Companies Act (board vs shareholders)?
column2: Board alone up to 10% of paid-up equity + free reserves; up to 25% needs a special resolution.

column1: Post buy-back debt-equity ratio limit?
column2: Total secured and unsecured debt must not exceed twice the paid-up capital and free reserves (2:1) after buy-back.

column1: In ESOP accounting, what is the intrinsic value method?
column2: Employee cost = excess of market price over the exercise price on the grant date, spread over the vesting period.

column1: What happens to securities premium on forfeiture of shares?
column2: Premium already received is retained; premium not received is cancelled — you can't reverse what was collected.

column1: On reissue of forfeited shares, where does the surplus go?
column2: To Capital Reserve — it's a capital profit, not a trading gain.

column1: Purpose of Internal Reconstruction (capital reduction)?
column2: To write off accumulated losses and overvalued assets against sacrificed capital without liquidating the company.

column1: Where is the balance in Capital Reduction / Reconstruction A/c transferred?
column2: To Capital Reserve after writing down all losses and fictitious assets.

column1: Why prepare a Realisation Account on dissolution of a partnership?
column2: To close all assets and outside liabilities and determine the profit or loss on realisation for distribution among partners.

column1: Order of payment under Insolvency (Section 53 IBC) waterfall — first priority?
column2: Insolvency resolution/liquidation costs, then secured creditors and workmen dues, before other stakeholders.

column1: What is the treatment of goodwill on a partner's admission?
column2: Incoming partner compensates sacrificing partners for their share of goodwill in the sacrificing ratio.

column1: Why prepare departmental accounts?
column2: To measure each department's profitability separately and allocate common costs on a rational basis.

column1: Independent vs dependent branch — key accounting difference?
column2: Independent branch keeps full double-entry books; a dependent branch's accounts are maintained by head office.

column1: In foreign branch translation, where do exchange differences usually go?
column2: To the profit and loss account (integral) or Foreign Currency Translation Reserve (non-integral).

column1: Insurance claim: why compute Gross Profit ratio for a loss of stock claim?
column2: To estimate the cost of stock destroyed via the trading account and derive the insurable loss.

column1: What does an average clause in a fire policy do?
column2: Penalises under-insurance — claim = loss × (policy value / actual stock value), so partial cover means partial recovery.

column1: Why maintain an Investment Account with separate cost and income columns?
column2: To distinguish capital (cost of investment) from revenue (interest/dividend) — cum vs ex interest treatment.

column1: Cum-interest vs ex-interest quotation — the difference?
column2: Cum-interest price includes accrued interest (deduct it from cost); ex-interest price excludes it (add accrued interest separately).

column1: For a bank, why classify advances into standard, sub-standard, doubtful, loss?
column2: Asset classification drives provisioning — riskier NPAs need higher provisions to reflect true recoverable value.

column1: When does an advance become an NPA (banking)?
column2: Interest/principal remains overdue for more than 90 days.

column1: Why do banks make provisions on standard assets too?
column2: To cover latent, not-yet-identified losses inherent in a performing portfolio — prudence at portfolio level.

column1: What is Rebate on Bills Discounted for a bank?
column2: Unexpired discount on bills maturing after year-end — income received but not yet earned, so it's a liability.

column1: Purpose of Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013?
column2: Prescribes the format of the balance sheet and statement of profit and loss for company financial statements.

column1: Why present a cash flow statement (AS 3)?
column2: To show how the enterprise generates and uses cash across operating, investing and financing activities — liquidity insight.

column1: Direct vs indirect method of cash flow (AS 3)?
column2: Direct shows gross cash receipts/payments; indirect starts from net profit and adjusts for non-cash and working-capital items.

column1: Why is the LLP conversion of a firm not treated as a sale?
column2: It's a continuation of the same business with limited liability; assets and liabilities carry over at book values.
